title: AI và quyền tự làm bài · Discuss both views
prompt: Some people support allowing university students to use generative AI in assessed coursework, while others oppose it because of the risks it could create. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
instructions: Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience. Write at least 250 words.

outline.purpose: Dạng discuss yêu cầu giải thích riêng vì sao mỗi phía tin lập trường của mình rồi đưa phán đoán của người viết. Trong bài này, cân nhắc trọng tâm là: So sánh đáp án AI với nguồn đáng tin buộc sinh viên tìm giả định sai và kiểm tra bằng chứng. Giá trị nằm ở hoạt động phê bình của người học, không phải tốc độ AI tạo văn bản. Điểm số có thể phản ánh năng lực công cụ thay vì năng lực người học. Khai báo tạo dấu vết sử dụng; vấn đáp kiểm tra người nộp có giải thích được quyết định trong bài không. Không biện pháp nào tự loại mọi gian lận.
outline.content: Supporters argue that aI assistance can support productive experimentation with ideas and language. Opponents respond that unrestricted assistance can conceal whether the student understands the submitted work. I accept the educational case for permitted AI use, but the objection about unreliable grades requires assessment to verify students' reasoning rather than reward the submitted text alone.

paragraphs: Supporters argue that aI assistance can support productive experimentation with ideas and language. Opponents respond that unrestricted assistance can conceal whether the student understands the submitted work. I accept the educational case for permitted AI use, but the objection about unreliable grades requires assessment to verify students' reasoning rather than reward the submitted text alone.

AI assistance can support productive experimentation with ideas and language. Comparing a generated answer with reliable sources exposes assumptions that students might otherwise overlook. A student could critique an AI explanation and submit a record of the errors identified. The learning activity is the comparison and correction, so access to a fluent answer is not equivalent to acquiring the understanding behind it. The educational benefit depends on students checking the output themselves; submitting a polished answer without that scrutiny demonstrates little independent understanding.

Unrestricted assistance can conceal whether the student understands the submitted work. An assessor normally treats the submitted reasoning as evidence of the student's ability. If a tool supplies that reasoning and the student cannot explain it, a high-quality product can produce an inaccurate judgement of independent competence. Universities should require disclosure and use short oral defences to verify understanding. Disclosure makes the process visible, while an oral defence tests whether the student can explain choices that a submitted text alone cannot verify. Assessment should distinguish the quality of the submitted product from the student's ability to explain, challenge and defend the reasoning behind it.

Both views identify a real feature of AI: it can stimulate inquiry or replace it, so disclosure and oral explanation make conditional permission more defensible than either unrestricted use or prohibition.
